## Question
When and where did Elijah Wilkins (born about 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky) die?

## Conclusion (Possible)
The evidence gathered so far points to Elijah Wilkins having died after 1870 and before the 1885 term of the Muhlenberg County court, most likely in Muhlenberg County, Kentucky. This is a bounded finding, not an exact date. An exact date is not established by the evidence gathered so far; it remains unresolved pending the 1880 census, estate settlement papers, and burial or newspaper records.

## Evidence
**Estate administration.** The Muhlenberg County Court order book for the 1885 term records the administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, with Jesse Wilkins as administrator (Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, Court Order Books, administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, Jesse Wilkins administrator, 1885 term; digital images, FamilySearch.org). This is a derivative index of the order-book page; the original order book was not separately imaged in this search. The record states no death date, so the death is inferred as before the administration (information quality indeterminate, informant the county clerk, record basis inferred). Jesse Wilkins is the subject's son in the tree (relationship R1), and his role as administrator anchors the decedent to the subject. That identity rests on the shared name, the county, and the son's role. The administrator persona is not itself linked to Jesse's tree person.

**Lower bound.** Existing tree fact F2 (Residence, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, 1870) places Elijah alive in 1870 and sets the lower bound. F2 carries no linked source entry in research.json.

**Documented negative.** A search of the Kentucky statewide death collections found nothing (12 results examined). That is expected: Kentucky statewide death registration began in 1911, so no death certificate exists for a man who died before 1885.

## Limits and conflicts
No conflicts are registered. The 15-year bracket is wide. Place of death is inferred from the venue of the estate court, not stated. The 1880 census for Muhlenberg County has not been searched; it would narrow the bracket itself, which is why the tier stays at possible. Estate inventory and settlement papers, will books, cemetery records and newspapers are also unsearched.

## Question
What was the maiden surname of Ellen (born about 1868), who married Michael Doyle on 12 June 1889 in Dubuque, Dubuque County, Iowa?

## Conclusion
Not proved. The maiden surname is not established by the evidence gathered so far, and no candidate surname has been identified.

## Evidence
The only record gathered is the Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate of Michael Doyle and Ellen, 12 June 1889, cited as: "Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate, Michael Doyle and Ellen [surname illegible], 12 June 1889; Dubuque County Recorder, digital image, FamilySearch." (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MDOYLE-1889). It is an original record. Its information on the marriage and on the groom's name is primary, stated directly by the bride and groom reporting to the county recorder, and it is direct evidence of the marriage event. The bride's given name, Ellen, is legible. Her surname, and her parents' names, are illegible in the register image because of the clerk's hand and fading. The one search made (FamilySearch, surname Doyle, given Michael, marriage) returned only this record.

The record identifies the bride as the tree's Ellen Doyle and the groom as Michael Doyle. There are no conflicting sources, since there is no second source to conflict. The question's single source cannot answer the question, so there is nothing to weigh and no basis to prefer any surname.

## What could resolve it
The maiden surname remains unresolved pending records not yet searched: later censuses showing the household; Ellen Doyle's death certificate or obituary naming her parents; Catholic parish baptism and burial registers in Dubuque; baptism or birth records of the couple's children giving the mother's maiden name; the marriage license application, the county marriage register entry, and newspaper marriage notices; and an alternative image or index transcription of this certificate. Any of these could name the surname directly, so the search is not at its ceiling.

## Tier
Not proved: one original record, illegible at the target field, with no independent corroboration. Nothing is encoded in the tree beyond the existing marriage and persons, because no surname conclusion exists.

## Conclusion

The evidence indicates that Anders Monsen (LKFW-9XH) married Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX) on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway. This finding is rated **probable**.

## Evidence

The single source is a marriage entry in "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register. It is a derivative index of an original church book entry. The information is primary and direct: the officiating minister or parish clerk recorded it on official duty at the time, and it states the date, place, groom (Anders Monsen) and bride. The index gives the bride as 'Urna Halsteinsdr'. This is read as a transcription variant of Unna Halsteinsdatter, since her christening of 27 May 1745 at Hamre carries the name Unna Halsteinsdatter in the tree (fact unna-christening-1; the tree carries no linked source entry for that fact). The groom was christened at Hamre on 7 April 1759 per tree fact anders-christening-1, so a marriage in the same parish is consistent. The tree already joined the couple (Couple rel-anders-unna) before this record; the record supplies the date and place.

## Conflicts and limits

No conflicting evidence is registered or known. The bride was about 14 years older than the groom, which is unusual but not impossible. Identity rests on matching names, parish and the existing couple link. The tier is probable rather than proved because the conclusion rests on one derivative index. The original Hamre church book, available through Digitalarkivet or a FamilySearch image, has not been examined. It would corroborate the date and place and could confirm the bride's name form. Research is not declared complete in that respect.

Proofs are never final, and a later reading of the original register could revise this.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Was Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)? An unsourced online family tree names him as the father and cites no record.

## Conclusion
Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry was not Patrick Flynn's father. The parish register shows Thomas buried on 14 November 1842. Two independent sources place Patrick's birth about 1845, so Thomas died about three years before Patrick was born. This **disproves** the online tree's claim for this candidate. It says nothing about who Patrick's parents actually were.

## Evidence
**Thomas's death.** The Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842. This is an original register entry, made by the officiating priest in the course of his duties, so the information is primary and directly stated. The research log notes that the townland, an approximate age of 42 and a wife named Bridget match the man the online tree describes. That match is what ties this burial to the Thomas Flynn the tree names. Citation: Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

**Patrick's birth.** The 1850 census lists Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of the widow Bridget Flynn, with no adult male Flynn present. Citation: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. The census is an original source, but its informant is unknown, so the age is indeterminate in quality and the birth year (about 1845) is an inference. The 1908 death certificate gives an age of about 63. Citation: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026. The informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, who was not present at his birth, so the age is secondary information and the year is calculated. The certificate names no father. The two sources were created about 58 years apart by different informants, and both point to about 1845.

## Analysis
A child can be born after the father's death, but only within roughly nine months, which here means by about August 1843. Both age statements would need to be wrong by about two years, in the same direction, to fit that window. Census and death-certificate ages are often imprecise, but they are independent, and neither suggests a birth before 1843. The widowed mother in 1850 is consistent with a father who died before Patrick was born or while he was young. It does not identify the father. The widow Bridget could be the wife of Thomas of Ballingarry, but nothing in the records shows that she is Patrick's mother. No conflicting evidence exists and no conflict is registered.

## Limits
The refutation holds for Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry only. The tie between the 1842 burial and the Thomas Flynn the tree names rests on matching townland, age and wife's name. If a different Thomas Flynn of the same place were meant, this conclusion would not apply to him. A baptismal entry for Patrick would settle his birth date directly, and a record naming his mother would help identify his actual parents. Like any proof, this conclusion is open to revision on new evidence.

## Tier
Disproved. The primary burial record and two independent age statements agree, and no conflict is open.

Citation: Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

**Patrick's birth.** The 1850 census lists Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of the widow Bridget Flynn, with no adult male Flynn present. Citation: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. The census is an original source, but its informant is unknown, so the age is indeterminate in quality and the birth year (about 1845) is an inference. The 1908 death certificate gives an age of about 63. Citation: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026. The informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, who was not present at his birth, so the age is secondary information and the year is calculated. The certificate names no father. The two sources were created about 58 years apart by different informants, and both point to about 1845.

## Analysis
A child can be born after the father's death, but only within roughly nine months, which here means by about August 1843. Both age statements would need to be wrong by about two years, in the same direction, to fit that window. Census and death-certificate ages are often imprecise, but they are independent, and neither suggests a birth before 1843. The widowed mother in 1850 is consistent with a father who died before Patrick was born or while he was young. It does not identify the father. The widow Bridget could be the wife of Thomas of Ballingarry, but nothing in the records shows that she is Patrick's mother. No conflicting evidence exists and no conflict is registered.

## Limits
The refutation holds for Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry only. The tie between the 1842 burial and the Thomas Flynn the tree names rests on matching townland, age and wife's name. If a different Thomas Flynn of the same place were meant, this conclusion would not apply to him. A baptismal entry for Patrick would settle his birth date directly, and a record naming his mother would help identify his actual parents. Like any proof, this conclusion is open to revision on new evidence.

## Tier
Disproved. The primary burial record and two independent age statements agree, and no conflict is open.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Conclusion

The evidence indicates that Anders Monsen (b. 1759, christened 7 April 1759 at Hamre kirke; tree fact anders-christening-1) married Unna Halsteinsdatter (christened 27 May 1745, Hamre; tree fact unna-christening-1) on **25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway**. This is a probable conclusion, not a proved one.

## Evidence

The sole source is a FamilySearch index entry for the marriage, "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register. The index names the groom as Anders Monsen and the bride as "Urna Halsteinsdr", and gives the date 25 June 1786 and place Hamre.

- **Classification.** The source is a derivative index of an original church book. The information (date, place, names) is primary: it was recorded at the time by the officiating minister or parish clerk acting in an official capacity, and the event is stated directly, so the evidence is direct. Both parties' names are stated by the register itself.
- **Identity.** The groom matches Anders Monsen exactly by name and sex, and the marriage took place in Hamre, the parish where he was christened in 1759. The bride's indexed form "Urna Halsteinsdr" is read as a transcription variant of Unna Halsteinsdatter: the patronymic matches, and her christening of 27 May 1745 at Hamre gives the name as Unna Halsteinsdatter. The tree already joined the couple (relationship rel-anders-unna) but carried no marriage date or place.
- **Plausibility.** She was about 41 and he 27 at the marriage. That is an unusual age gap but not impossible, and nothing in the record conflicts with it. No conflicting evidence was found.

## Image availability

The request for this conclusion asked that the narrative state that the register image is digitized and accessible on FamilySearch. The project data do not support that. The search response carried no image reference, no image count was reported, and record_read was never called to check. The ARK cited is a record-level (1:1:) identifier, not a confirmed image identifier. This conclusion therefore rests on the index entry only, and the existence of a digitized page is unconfirmed.

## Tier

Probable. Only one source supports the answer, and it is an index (derivative) rather than the original register or its image. Because no civil registration existed in 1786, no independent record type is expected to exist; the church book is the sole contemporaneous record. The gap is that the register page itself has not been viewed. Viewing it (via record_read, or the Hamre church book through the Digitalarkivet or FamilySearch catalog) would verify the transcription, including the bride's name variant, and could lift the conclusion to proved.

## Question

What was the maiden surname of Ellen (born about 1868), who married Michael Doyle on 12 June 1889 in Dubuque, Dubuque County, Iowa?

## Finding

The maiden surname is not established by the evidence gathered so far. The tier is **not proved**, and the question stays open.

## Evidence

Only one record has been gathered: the Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate of Michael Doyle and Ellen, 12 June 1889 (Dubuque County Recorder, digital image, FamilySearch; citation: "Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate, Michael Doyle and Ellen [surname illegible], 12 June 1889; Dubuque County Recorder, digital image, FamilySearch."). It is an original record, and its information is primary: the bride and groom were their own informants. It states directly that Ellen married Michael Doyle on that date and place. Her given name is legible. Her surname, and her parents' names, are illegible in the image because of the clerk's hand and fading. The record therefore gives no usable answer to the question. No other record names her, and no conflicting evidence exists.

## Why this is not closed

The project's exhaustiveness declaration rests on the certificate being the record of the event, but the same declaration records that only FamilySearch was searched, only for the marriage, and that nothing independent corroborates it. An illegible image does not show that the surname cannot be found. Several record types that routinely give a married woman's maiden name were not searched: death certificates or obituaries for Ellen and her children, the 1895 and 1905 Iowa and 1900 and 1910 federal censuses for the household, Catholic baptismal records of the children (with sponsors), children's birth records, Michael Doyle's probate file, and a separately viewed register or index entry for the marriage. Any of these could settle the surname. The finding stays at not proved with a remediable gap, rather than being recorded as unanswerable.

## Tree

Nothing was encoded for the maiden surname; there is no value to write. The marriage of Ellen and Michael Doyle is already in the tree.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of John Richardson (Utah pioneer, d. 10 March 1906, Richmond, Cache, Utah)

**Conclusion (probable).** The evidence strongly indicates that John Richardson was the son of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu. It is not stated as established fact because the christening register's year (1832) disagrees with the tree's birth and christening year (1833), and that disagreement bears on whether the christened child is the Utah pioneer.

**Question note.** The question as framed says baptised 25 September 1833. The original register reads 25 September 1832.

### Direct evidence
The original Ashton-under-Lyne baptism register, entry no. 2040, reads: "September 25 — John — Thomas X Richardson, Mary — Town — Spinner — J. Hardman" (original record, primary information, direct evidence; recorded by the officiating curate in the course of duty). It names Thomas Richardson, a spinner who signed by mark, and Mary as John's parents. Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org : accessed 22 July 2026), St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, baptism register, pp. 254–255, entry no. 2040, John, son of Thomas Richardson and Mary, 25 September 1832; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm 4421674.

The FamilySearch index "England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975" (derivative, secondary information, indexer as informant) gives the same christening, with father Thomas Richardson and mother Mary, and also reads 25 Sep 1832. It repeats the original rather than independently confirming it.

### Mother's surname
The register gives the mother only as Mary. The original Walton le Dale marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, records Thos Richardson (bachelor) and Mary Mallalieu (spinster) marrying by banns on 12 November 1826, both signing by mark, witnessed by John Quarmen and James Townson (original record, primary information for the marriage). Citation: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm. Both couples' husbands signed by mark, and the marriage precedes the baptism by about six years. This is indirect evidence that the Mary of the baptism is Mary Mallalieu. The identification rests on matching names, the husband's mark and spinner occupation, and Lancashire location. No record states it outright, and the two parishes are about 35 miles apart.

### Unresolved point: the year
The tree carries John's birth as 24 July 1833 at Preston and a christening of 25 September 1833. Those tree facts have no source entry in the project, apart from the christening fact, which cites the 1832 register. A christening in September 1832 cannot belong to a child born in July 1833. Either the tree's 1833 is wrong, or the christened John is a different child. The match of name, day, month and church favours the first, and no other John Richardson christening at Ashton-under-Lyne was found (log_002, log_003). This is not registered as a conflict in the project, and I have not resolved it. It is the reason the finding stops at probable.

### Limits
No independent record of John's own birth year or birthplace has been brought in. Plan items still open are listed in the search summary. Findings remain open to revision on new evidence.

- **Next step:** run conflict-resolution on the year discrepancy, then research-plan to search the records above for an independent birth year. The narrative runs about 47 words over the summary budget.

Records that independently fix his birth year and place have not been searched, such as Utah death and census records, church records, and Preston-area baptisms, and some planned searches, including Ancestry, are still open.

This research is finished for now. If you'd like a second opinion on it, just ask.

entry.narrative_markdown:
# Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. about 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)

**Conclusion (probable).** The evidence indicates that Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn (born about 1818, Ireland) of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. No record found so far names Patrick's mother, so that half of the question remains unanswered.

## Evidence

**1908 death certificate (direct, secondary information).** Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026. The record is an original, and it states the father as Thomas Flynn. The informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, who was not present at Patrick's birth and was reporting what he had been told decades later. The information about parentage is therefore secondary. It is nonetheless a direct, stated answer to the question.

**1850 census (indirect).** 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026. Patrick appears in Thomas Flynn's household. The 1850 census does not state relationships, so the parent-child link is inferred from household position and shared surname. The informant is unidentified, and the information is of indeterminate quality. An Ancestry index of the same census (a derivative) is consistent with it and adds no independent weight.

**1860 census (indirect).** 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Patrick, age 15, is again in Thomas Flynn's household. Relationships are still not stated, so this is indirect evidence of the same kind as 1850.

The two censuses are separate original records from different enumerations, but they share a likely informant (Thomas or his wife), and both rest on the same inference. They are consistent with the death certificate, and the three together make Thomas the strongest candidate. A common surname in a county with many Irish immigrants limits how much co-residence alone can show.

## Conflict

Conflict c_001 concerns Patrick's birthplace: Ireland in both censuses and Pennsylvania on the death certificate. It is resolved in favour of Ireland, because the censuses were contemporary and the death certificate informant was a son-in-law with no first-hand knowledge. The disagreement does not call into question whether the records describe the same man, since the name, county, age and household match throughout. It does not touch the parentage conclusion.

## Limits

No record states the relationship directly from a first-hand informant, so the tier is probable and not proved. Research is not declared exhaustive. Unsearched and reachable records that could corroborate the father or identify the mother are the 1870 and 1880 censuses (1880 records relationships), baptism or parish records, Schuylkill County probate files, naturalization records and obituaries. These would mostly corroborate the father; the mother can only be named by one of them. This conclusion could change if such records appear.

**Tier: probable (father: Thomas Flynn). Mother: not identified.**

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question

Was Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)? An unsourced online family tree names him as the father.

## Conclusion

The claim is disproved for this man. Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry was buried on 14 November 1842, about three years before Patrick Flynn was born. He cannot be Patrick's father. The scope is limited to this candidate: the evidence says nothing yet about who Patrick's parents were.

## Evidence

**Thomas's death.** The Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842 (original register, primary information, entered by the officiating priest in the course of his duty; direct evidence of death). Source: Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026. The entry matches the man the online tree describes (townland, approximate age, and wife Bridget), so it concerns the same Thomas, not a namesake.

**Patrick's birth.** Two independent original records place Patrick's birth about 1845. The 1850 census lists Patrick, age 5, in the household of widow Bridget Flynn, with no adult male Flynn present (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). The informant there is unknown, so the age is of indeterminate quality, and the birth year is inferred from it. His 1908 death certificate gives age about 63 (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026). The informant was his son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at Patrick's birth, so this is secondary information. Neither record names a father.

## Weighing

Both ages are imprecise, and ages in census and death records are often off by a year or two. Even a generous error would put Patrick's birth no earlier than about 1843, still after the November 1842 burial. Two independent sources agree, and no source disagrees, so there is no conflict to resolve. A posthumous birth would need a birth within about nine months of the burial, which both ages exclude. The parentage claim carries no cited record, so nothing contradicts this finding.

## Limits

The widow Bridget Flynn in the 1850 census is suggestive but not shown to be the Bridget named in the online tree; this does not affect the finding. Patrick's real parents are not identified. This finding is open to revision only if a record shows a different man of the same name, which would be a different candidate, not this one. Unsearched for the wider question: Patrick's baptism, his marriage record, and obituary or church records.

The proof-conclusion agent reviewed ps_001 as it stands and produced this verdict:

---

### Tier: Probable — correct, but not yet GPS-compliant

**Probable is right; Proved is not yet warranted.** The census evidence is inferred from household position, not stated relationship, and the only direct naming comes from a secondary informant (son-in-law). Possible would be too low, as three consistent items converge on Thomas Flynn as father. The resolved conflict c_001 (birthplace) does not cap the tier.

---

### Five GPS Components

1. **Exhaustive search — NOT MET.** ps_001 itself acknowledges the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses are unsearched and probate is "in progress." This is the clearest GPS shortfall.

2. **Complete, accurate citations — MET.** The three citations match the stored source entries verbatim and each carries an original classification.

3. **Analysis and correlation — MOSTLY MET, with two weaknesses:**
   - *Overstated independence.* The narrative calls these "three independent lines," but the 1850 and 1860 censuses are the same household and likely the same informant. They constitute one line enumerated twice.
   - *Unsupported age detail.* The narrative gives Thomas's age as 32 and birth as Ireland, but neither fact appears in ps_001's cited assertions (a_004, a_010, a_013).

4. **Conflict resolution — MET, with a caveat.** The Ireland-vs.-Pennsylvania birthplace reasoning is sound (two contemporary records outrank a son-in-law's later recollection). However, resolution rests on the assumption that the census Patrick is the same Patrick who died in 1908 — plausible but untested without a baptism record.

5. **Coherent written conclusion — MOSTLY MET.** The narrative is self-contained and uses conditional phrasing appropriate to Probable. One structural gap: the question asks for *parents* (plural), yet the conclusion addresses only the father and never states that the mother is unidentified.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Assessment of ps_001 (q_001, parentage of Patrick Flynn): it holds at probable and does not meet the Genealogical Proof Standard.** I changed nothing in the project.

### Tier
- **Probable is the right tier.** The rating cannot go up to proved. The census evidence is only inferred from household position, and the one direct statement comes from a secondary informant. The search is also openly incomplete.
- **Possible would be too low.** There are three consistent items: the 1850 census, the 1860 census, and the 1908 death certificate naming Thomas Flynn as father.
- **Conflict c_001 does not cap the tier.** It concerns birthplace and is resolved, with no questions blocked.

### The five components
1. **Exhaustive research: not met.** ps_001 admits that the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses are unsearched and that probate is only "in progress". The shortfall is correctly marked "gap".
2. **Citations: met.** The three citations match the stored source entries verbatim, and each source carries an original classification.
3. **Analysis and correlation: mostly met, with two weaknesses.**
   - **Overstated independence.** The narrative says "three independent lines of evidence". But the 1850 and 1860 censuses are the same household and probably the same informant, and conflict c_001 itself says so. They are better treated as one line of evidence enumerated twice.
   - **Missing support for the father's age.** The narrative gives Thomas as age 32, born Ireland. Neither fact is among ps_001's cited supporting assertions (a_004, a_010, a_013). The Thomas name assertion a_005 is linked to the question but not cited either.
4. **Conflicts: met, with a caveat.** The reasoning for choosing Ireland over Pennsylvania is sound. Two contemporary records outrank a son-in-law's later recollection, and the narrative explains why he may have been wrong. Birthplace does bear on identity, though. The resolution is only as strong as the assumption that the census Patrick is the Patrick who died in 1908. That is plausible given matching ages and household, but a baptism record would test it directly.
5. **Coherent narrative: mostly met.** It is self-contained, uses conditional phrasing consistent with probable, and names informants. One gap is that the question asks for parents (plural). The narrative concludes only the father and never says the mother is unidentified. The tree has Thomas Flynn linked as Patrick's father but no mother. It also links Mary and James Flynn as Thomas's children, and ps_001 does not cite evidence for them.

### Tree
The father-child link from Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn is encoded, which is appropriate at probable. The question is still marked in progress in the project even though a proof exists. I have not changed that.

### Evidence gaps for the next round
Five sources are in the project but have no assertions extracted, so ps_001 does not use them. These are gaps in coverage, not defects in ps_001.
- **St. Mary's, Pottsville baptism, 1845 (src_005).** This is the most important one. If it names the parents, it is direct evidence close to the birth. It would also test the Ireland versus Pennsylvania conflict and could reopen or settle it. It could move the tier toward proved, or change the answer.
- **Thomas Flynn's will, 1881 (src_006).** If it names Patrick as a son, it is the direct probate evidence ps_001 says it is waiting for. It could raise the tier.
- **Deed from Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn, 1881 (src_008).** It would show a transaction between the two. Unless the deed states a relationship, it is indirect support only.
- **1908 obituary (src_009).** It may name the parents or survivors. It would be useful corroboration but probably not enough alone to change the tier.
- **1905 birth certificate for Mary Elizabeth Flynn (src_007).** It likely concerns a grandchild and is probably peripheral. It could help with the mother or the family structure.
- **Other searches.** The 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses are still unsearched. The 1880 census is the first to state relationships, so it would give the first direct relationship statement. It would corroborate and could narrow the answer to include the mother.

Extracting and classifying src_005 and src_006 is the highest-value next step. The searches would be planned through research-plan. Those two together could plausibly support proved, provided the birthplace conflict stays resolved.

---

The research suggests Patrick Flynn was probably the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. That rests on two censuses, 1850 and 1860, that list Patrick in Thomas's household at ages that fit, and on Patrick's 1908 death certificate, where his son-in-law named Thomas as his father. The censuses do not state relationships, and the son-in-law was reporting from hearsay, so the finding is likely but not firmly established. Nothing has yet identified Patrick's mother. A thorough search has not yet covered several records already located: the 1845 baptism, Thomas's 1881 will, an 1881 deed between Thomas and Patrick, and the 1908 obituary. The 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses are also unsearched.

The next step is to read and classify the baptism and the will, since they could confirm or overturn the finding.

**Assessment of ps\_001 — Parentage of Patrick Flynn**

The proof-conclusion agent reviewed ps\_001 against all five GPS components. Here is what it found.

---

### Overall Verdict

**ps\_001 (rated "Probable") is defensible at that tier, but does not yet meet the Genealogical Proof Standard.** The conclusion — *Patrick Flynn is probably the son of Thomas Flynn* — is fair given the evidence cited, but the written proof has significant presentation gaps.

---

### GPS Component-by-Component

**Component 1 — Reasonably Exhaustive Search**
Not met. The proof acknowledges that the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses are unsearched and that probate is "in progress." Several located records have no extraction yet. The shortfall makes the search incomplete, not exhaustive.

**Component 2 — Complete, Accurate Citations**
Partially met. The source entries (src\_001, src\_003, src\_004) carry complete citations, but the proof narrative contains no citations at all — only bare internal IDs (a\_004, a\_010, a\_013). A reader without the project files cannot follow it. GPS requires the narrative itself to be self-contained.

**Component 3 — Thorough Analysis and Correlation**
Weak. The three cited assertions largely repeat one inference:
- **1850 and 1860 censuses (a\_004, a\_010):** household placement; neither census states a relationship, both are indeterminate.
- **1908 death certificate (a\_013):** names Thomas Flynn as father, but the informant was a son-in-law — secondary information.

No source provides a primary, direct statement of parentage. The analysis is not wrong, but it is thin.

**Component 4 — Resolution of All Conflicting Evidence**
Partially met. Conflict c\_001 (birthplace: Ireland vs. Pennsylvania) is cited and marked resolved in favour of Ireland. However, the narrative only says the conflict was resolved "in favour of the earlier of the two record groups" without naming the attribute, the records, or the reasoning. That is insufficient for self-containment.

**Component 5 — Soundly Reasoned, Coherent Written Conclusion**
Not met. The narrative names evidence only by internal IDs, never states record dates, repositories, or informant classifications (original/derivative, primary/secondary, direct/indirect), and the "what would advance it" section names no specific record types.

---

### Tier Assessment

| Tier | Why |
|------|-----|
| **Not Proved** | Ruled out — the records are consistent and nothing contradicts Thomas's paternity |
| **Possible** | Ruled out — independent record types agree |
| ✅ **Probable** | Correct — consistent agreement across record types, but no primary direct statement of parentage |
| **Proved** | Not yet — requires a primary direct source (baptism, will naming Patrick as heir, or a 1880 census "son" relationship) |

---

### Evidence Gaps (not defects — next-round work)

These sources exist in the project but are **not cited in ps\_001**. They are gaps for future work. Several could change the tier:

| Source | Status | Tier Impact |
|--------|--------|-------------|
| **1845 baptism, St. Mary's, Pottsville (src\_005)** | No assertions extracted | **Could lift to Proved** if it names Thomas as father; also reopens the birthplace conflict (Pennsylvania, not Ireland) |
| **Will of Thomas Flynn, 1881 (src\_006)** | Not extracted | **Could lift to Proved** if Patrick is named as son |
| **1880 census** | Not searched | **Could lift to Proved** — first census to record stated relationships ("son") |
| Deed, Thomas to Patrick, 1881 (src\_008) | Not extracted | Corroborating only; would not raise tier alone |
| Obituary, 1908 (src\_009) | Not extracted | Secondary; corroborating only |
| 1870 census | Not searched | Corroborating; would not raise tier alone |

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Extract the 1845 baptism (src\_005)** — highest priority; could prove parentage directly and may reopen the birthplace conflict.
2. **Extract Thomas Flynn's 1881 will (src\_006)** — could name Patrick as a son.
3. **Search the 1870 and 1880 censuses** — the 1880 census states relationships directly.
4. **Rewrite ps\_001** so the narrative names and cites each record, states informant classifications, and spells out the conflict resolution reasoning.

agent_returns.text:
**Assessment of ps_001 (q_001, parentage of Patrick Flynn)**

I read the proof, its three supporting assertions, the conflict it cites, the sources and the research log. I wrote nothing. This is a review only, and no persisted artifact comes out of it.

**Overall:** ps_001 is rated probable, and that tier is defensible. It does not meet the Genealogical Proof Standard, and the proof itself says so. As written, it is weak on reader-facing documentation. Its conclusion is "Patrick Flynn is probably the son of Thomas Flynn."

**1. Tier.**
- **Why probable holds:**
  - The 1850 and 1860 census household placements (a_004, a_010) are inferred. Neither census states relationships, and both are classed as indeterminate.
  - The 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father (a_013). It is an original record, but the informant was a son-in-law, so the information is secondary.
  - Nothing cited contradicts the link.
- **Why not proved:**
  - There is no primary, direct statement of parentage.
  - Research is not declared exhaustive.
  - The three items largely repeat one inference. The two censuses rest on household position and shared surname, and the death certificate rests on a son-in-law's hearsay.
- **Why not possible:** the independent record types agree, and no source disputes the father. Probable is right, and it is not a generous reading.
- **Mother:** none is named, so the finding covers the father only.

**2. Self-containment.** This check fails.
- The narrative names its evidence only by bare ids: a_004, a_010, a_013, src_001, src_003, src_004, c_001 and plan_001.
- It never names the 1850 or 1860 census, the death certificate, the informant James Brown, or any record date or repository.
- A reader without the project files cannot follow it.
- It also never states the three-layer classification: original or derivative, primary or secondary, direct or indirect.

**3. Citations.** The narrative contains none. The stored citations for src_001, src_003 and src_004 are complete and could be copied in. Because the narrative cites nothing, GPS component 2 is met in the sources section but not in the proof as written.

**4. Conflicts.**
- c_001 (birthplace) is cited and its status is resolved. The census records say Ireland and the death certificate says Pennsylvania. The resolution prefers Ireland.
- The narrative only says it was resolved "in favour of the earlier of the two record groups". It does not name the attribute or give the reasoning.
- The birthplace bears on identity, so it needs to be stated. a_002 and a_012, the census and death-certificate birthplaces, are not among the supporting assertions.
- The census informants are probably the same person, so the two censuses are not fully independent on birthplace. The conflict entry notes this, but the narrative does not.

**5. Exhaustiveness.**
- The summary lists the 1850 census (log_001 to log_003), the 1860 census (log_004) and the death certificate (log_005). It says the probate search is "in progress" and that the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses are not searched.
- It cites log ids only, and it mentions MyHeritage, which has no source entry in the project.
- Only log_004 and log_005 came back under q_001.
- The shortfall of "gap" is correct, since reachable records remain.

**6. Unresolvability claims.** There are none, which is good. The "what would advance it" line points only at "the records named in the plan" and names no record type. That is a vagueness problem, not a forbidden claim.

**7. Tree.**
- Thomas Flynn (I2) is linked as parent of Patrick (I1), and also of Mary (I3) and James (I4).
- That matches a probable tier.
- The tree has no mother.
- I did not check the source references on the relationship edge.
- The question status still reads in progress, and the project flags "concluded while blocked: re-conclude ps_001". The cause of the block is not recorded in the proof.

**Gaps for the next round.** These sources exist in the project but ps_001 does not cite them. They are not defects of the current proof.
- **1845 baptism, St. Mary's, Pottsville (src_005):**
  - It is an original record and could name the parents directly.
  - It has no assertions extracted yet.
  - It could lift the tier to proved if it names Thomas.
  - It also places the baptism in Pennsylvania, which fits the death certificate's birthplace and cuts against c_001's choice of Ireland. If extraction confirms that, the conflict should be re-examined.
- **Will of Thomas Flynn, 1881 (src_006):** it likely lists heirs. A will naming Patrick as son would be strong corroboration and could raise the tier.
- **Deed, Thomas to Patrick, 1881 (src_008):** indirect only. It would support a family link, but it would not raise the tier on its own.
- **Obituary, Pottsville Republican, 1908 (src_009):** this is likely secondary information about parentage. It would corroborate but probably not change the tier.
- **Birth certificate of Mary Elizabeth Flynn, 1905 (src_007):** it has little bearing on Patrick's parents.
- **1870 and 1880 censuses:** the 1880 census is the first to state relationships directly. It could give a direct statement of "son" if Patrick was still in or near Thomas's household.

The baptism, the will and the 1880 census are the records that could change the tier. All four unextracted sources also still carry rough working citations that need cleaning up.

**Next step:** re-conclude ps_001 after extracting the baptism and will, using research-plan for the 1870 and 1880 census searches.

---

Patrick Flynn very likely was the son of Thomas Flynn. Two census listings put Patrick in Thomas's household, and his 1908 death certificate names Thomas as his father. The certificate was filled out by his son-in-law, who was not an eyewitness to the birth. The census listings only imply the relationship from who lived in the house. So the finding is likely but not firmly established, and the written explanation is hard for an outsider to follow because it names records only by internal labels. Records not yet searched or read include the 1870 and 1880 censuses and probate. Several records already located have not been analyzed yet: the 1845 baptism, Thomas's 1881 will, an 1881 deed, and the 1908 obituary.

The next step is to extract the baptism and will, search the 1870 and 1880 censuses, and then rewrite the conclusion so it names and cites each record.

entry.narrative_markdown:
# Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ca. 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)

**Question.** Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn?

**Answer.** The evidence strongly suggests that Patrick's father was Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County (probable). Patrick's mother is not established by the evidence gathered so far; the proposal that she was the widow Bridget Flynn is unsupported (not proved) and is not encoded.

## Paternity: Thomas Flynn (probable)

Three items point to Thomas.

1. **1850 census.** A Patrick Flynn is enumerated in the household of Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026). This is an original source, but the 1850 census states no relationships. The parent-child reading is inferred from household position and shared surname: indirect evidence, information quality indeterminate. The Ancestry index of the same census (src_002) is a derivative of this record and adds no independent weight.
2. **1860 census.** Patrick Flynn, age 15, is again in a Thomas Flynn household (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026). Again an original source with an inferred relationship, because 1860 also did not record relationships. The age is consistent with the 1850 entry. The two censuses are two enumerations, but the same household reporting is likely, so they corroborate co-residence over ten years rather than act as fully independent proof of descent.
3. **1908 death certificate.** The certificate names Thomas Flynn as father (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026). It is an original record and the only item that directly states the relationship, but the informant was a son-in-law, James Brown, not present at the events and reporting second-hand: secondary information. Its source is plausibly family tradition, so it is not independent of what the household believed.

The three items are consistent and nothing contradicts them. The weight is moderate: two items rest on inference and the one direct statement is secondary, which is why this is probable rather than proved.

## Conflict accounted for

Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the censuses vs. Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved in favor of Ireland on the grounds that the contemporary census entries outweigh a secondary informant 63 years later. Birthplace is an identifying attribute, and the resolution keeps the census Patrick and the certificate Patrick as one person (same county, same name, consistent age). It does not affect the parentage reading, and the death certificate's Pennsylvania entry is treated as the son-in-law's error. If that resolution were wrong, the identity link between the censuses and the certificate would need to be revisited.

## Maternity: not proved

The only candidate is Bridget Flynn, enumerated as a 52-year-old widow, head of household, in the 1870 census (1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026). The record names no husband and no child, and Thomas Flynn does not appear in 1870. Flynn is a common surname in the county, and the person-evidence link for her is speculative (match score 0.0002). No record names her as Thomas's wife or Patrick's mother. The 1870 and 1872 baptisms at St. Patrick's, Pottsville (src_006) name Patrick Flynn and Mary Doyle as parents of Patrick's own children, so Mary Doyle is most likely Patrick's wife and has no bearing on his mother. Maternity therefore remains unresolved pending the 1880 census, a marriage or baptism record naming Patrick's mother, Thomas Flynn's probate or burial record, or an obituary.

## Scope and limits

Research is not declared exhaustive; unsearched records are listed in the exhaustive-search summary. The unsearched records would mostly corroborate paternity, though a record naming the mother would answer the maternity claim itself. This conclusion is open to revision on new evidence.

Conflict c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in the censuses vs. Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved in favor of Ireland on the grounds that the contemporary census entries outweigh a secondary informant 63 years later. It does not affect the parentage reading, and the death certificate's Pennsylvania entry is treated as the son-in-law's error. If that resolution were wrong, the identity link between the censuses and the certificate would need to be revisited.

The only candidate is Bridget Flynn, enumerated as a 52-year-old widow, head of household, in the 1870 census (1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026). The 1870 and 1872 baptisms at St. Patrick's, Pottsville (src_006) name Patrick Flynn and Mary Doyle as parents of Patrick's own children, so Mary Doyle is most likely Patrick's wife and has no bearing on his mother. Maternity therefore remains unresolved pending the 1880 census, a marriage or baptism record naming Patrick's mother, Thomas Flynn's probate or burial record, or an obituary.

Research is not declared exhaustive; unsearched records are listed in the exhaustive-search summary. The unsearched records would mostly corroborate paternity, though a record naming the mother would answer the maternity claim itself. This conclusion is open to revision on new evidence.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Did Person A (born 1856, Germany) leave an accessible South Dakota death certificate, and when did Person A die?

## Conclusion
The evidence indicates that Person A probably died in 1935 at or near Gregory, Gregory County, South Dakota. An accessible death certificate was not found: none appears in FamilySearch's indexed South Dakota death records, and whether one exists remains unresolved pending a South Dakota State Archives vital-records request or a browse of unindexed FamilySearch death-certificate microfilm.

## Evidence
- **Find a Grave Index** entry, memorial #88075502, gives death 1935 and burial at Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota ("Find a Grave Index," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVLD-NSQ7 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, memorial #88075502). Derivative source; the contributor is unidentified, so information quality is indeterminate; the statement is direct for the death year but undated beyond the year.
- **South Dakota Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942** record burial at Gregory IOOF Cemetery, age at death 79, date of death blank ("South Dakota, Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942," database with images, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:CYCQ-NRW2 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota). An original government record, but the informant is unknown and the age is indirect evidence of the death year: with birth 1856 (existing tree fact F1, Birth, Germany, 1856; no linked source entry in research.json), age 79 points to 1935 or very early 1936 depending on the unknown birth date, and the record's creation in 1939-1942 sets an upper bound for the death.
- Existing tree fact F2 (Residence, Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota, 1935) places him in Gregory in 1935; it carries no linked source entry in research.json.

The two sources are not fully independent of each other in origin but were created separately, and they agree on place and on year (the age calculation is consistent with 1935). No conflicts are registered.

## Death certificate
Searches of FamilySearch-indexed South Dakota death records under two surname spelling variants returned no certificate (log_003, log_004, both negative). FamilySearch does not index every South Dakota certificate, so this is a limit of the index rather than evidence that none was issued; South Dakota had statewide death registration by 1935, so a certificate may well exist. It is not established by the evidence gathered so far, pending the State Archives request or unindexed microfilm browse.

## Tier and limits
Probable: consistent year and place from two sources, no conflicts, but both carry information of indeterminate quality and neither gives an exact date. A certificate would supply primary information and could refine or contradict 1935 (moderate overturn risk). The exact day remains unknown.

The proof-conclusion agent has completed its analysis and appended proof summary `ps_001`. Here's the finding:

---

## Conclusion: Who Was Patrick Flynn's Father?

**Tier: Not Proved — open question**

We cannot yet say who Patrick Flynn's father was. The research so far uncovered two separate Irish-born Patrick Flynns of roughly the right age in the 1850 census:
- **Age 5** in the household of **Thomas Flynn**
- **Age 6** in the household of **Michael Flynn**

Nothing in the evidence connects the adult Patrick Flynn to either household. The question remains open because:

- His **1908 death certificate** left the father's name **blank**
- The **1860 census** shows him as a teenage boarder with no relatives nearby
- A **parish baptism search** found no matching record
- The two candidates are competing hypotheses, not yet resolved

### Still Unsearched — Records That Could Narrow the Answer

| Record | Why It Helps |
|---|---|
| 1870 & 1880 censuses | May show Patrick living near a Flynn household |
| Marriage record | May name his father or place of origin |
| Children's death certificates | Often name the grandparents |
| Obituary & burial record | May name survivors or place of origin |
| Naturalization papers | Often include birthplace and parents |

**Recommended next step:** Use the **research-plan** agent to plan searches in those records. Any one of them could identify which Flynn household Patrick belonged to.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion (Not Proved).** The evidence gathered so far does not establish whether Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn or Michael Flynn, or neither. Two 1850 households fit equally well, and nothing yet links adult Patrick to either. The question remains open pending the marriage, children's death, census (1870/1880) and obituary records named below.

### The subject
Patrick Flynn died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. His death certificate is an original record with primary information about the death, supplied by the attending physician (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026). It identifies the subject unambiguously, but on the parentage point it is negative evidence: the father field is blank and the informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported the father's name as unknown. A son-in-law is a distant informant on a father-in-law's parentage, so this silence says little about whether a father was known to others.

### Competing candidates
A search of the 1850 census produced two Irish-born boys named Patrick Flynn of fitting age, both in Schuylkill County:

- Candidate A: age 5 (born ~1845) in the household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, family 91 (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026).
- Candidate B: age 6 (born ~1844) in the household of Michael Flynn, dwelling 210, family 233 (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026).

Both are original records, but the 1850 census does not state relationships, so a child's tie to the head is inferred from household position and the informant is unknown. The information is therefore of indeterminate quality and the relationship evidence is indirect. Age 5 versus 6 sits well within ordinary census age error for a subject born about 1845, so age does not favor A over B. Both Irish birthplaces match equally. Because nothing separates them, each candidate-father hypothesis is exactly as strong as the other, and neither is eliminated. Giving either a preference would be unsupported.

### The bridge that fails
The 1860 census shows a Patrick Flynn, age 15, as a boarder and coal laborer in the Owen Donnelly household, Schuylkill County, with no Flynn adult present (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026). This is the right age and county for the subject and is original, but it does not tie him to Thomas or Michael; neither appears as a near neighbor. It also shows that by age 15 he lived apart from any Flynn relative, which is consistent with, but does not prove, the loss or departure of a parent.

### Negative and unfound evidence
A search of FamilySearch and the National Library of Ireland Catholic parish registers (Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850) located no baptism naming a father. This is a not-found result in indexes of limited coverage, not evidence that no baptism exists.

### Why no tier above Not Proved
The only evidence naming any candidate father is the two 1850 household placements, which are equally weighted and indirect, and the identity of the child in each as the subject is unconfirmed. The personal links to both Thomas and Michael are speculative. No conflict is registered because the sources do not contradict each other; they simply fail to discriminate. Giving a probable or possible tier to either would require a reason to prefer one, and none exists in the record set. Neither name is encoded in the tree.

### What could settle it
The evidence gathered so far does not establish the father pending records not yet searched: the 1870 and 1880 censuses (in 1880 relationship and parents' birthplace are stated, and a co-resident relative could connect Patrick to household A or B), Patrick's marriage record, the death certificates of his children (which may name his father), his obituary and burial record, and naturalization papers. Any of these could name the father or link Patrick to one household. Conclusions are never final: a later record could change this finding.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion (Not Proved).** The evidence gathered so far does not establish whether Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn or Michael Flynn, or neither. Two 1850 households fit equally well, and nothing yet links adult Patrick to either. The question remains open pending the marriage, children's death, census (1870/1880) and obituary records named below.

### The subject
Patrick Flynn died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. His death certificate is an original record with primary information about the death, supplied by the attending physician (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026). It identifies the subject unambiguously, but on the parentage point it is negative evidence: the father field is blank and the informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported the father's name as unknown. A son-in-law is a distant informant on a father-in-law's parentage, so this silence says little about whether a father was known to others.

### Competing candidates
A search of the 1850 census produced two Irish-born boys named Patrick Flynn of fitting age, both in Schuylkill County:

- Candidate A: age 5 (born ~1845) in the household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, family 91 (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026).
- Candidate B: age 6 (born ~1844) in the household of Michael Flynn, dwelling 210, family 233 (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026).

Both are original records, but the 1850 census does not state relationships, so a child's tie to the head is inferred from household position and the informant is unknown. The information is therefore of indeterminate quality and the relationship evidence is indirect. Age 5 versus 6 sits well within ordinary census age error for a subject born about 1845, so age does not favor A over B. Both Irish birthplaces match equally. Because nothing separates them, each candidate-father hypothesis is exactly as strong as the other, and neither is eliminated. Giving either a preference would be unsupported.

### The bridge that fails
The 1860 census shows a Patrick Flynn, age 15, as a boarder and coal laborer in the Owen Donnelly household, Schuylkill County, with no Flynn adult present (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026). This is the right age and county for the subject and is original, but it does not tie him to Thomas or Michael; neither appears as a near neighbor.

### Negative and unfound evidence
A search of FamilySearch and the National Library of Ireland Catholic parish registers (Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850) located no baptism naming a father. This is a not-found result in indexes of limited coverage, not evidence that no baptism exists.

### Why no tier above Not Proved
The only evidence naming any candidate father is the two 1850 household placements, which are equally weighted and indirect, and the identity of the child in each as the subject is unconfirmed. The links of the child to both Thomas and Michael are speculative. No conflict is registered because the sources do not contradict each other; they simply fail to discriminate. A probable or possible tier for either would require a reason to prefer one, and none exists in the record set. Neither name is encoded in the tree.

### What could settle it
The evidence gathered so far does not establish the father pending records not yet searched: the 1870 and 1880 censuses (in 1880 relationship and parents' birthplace are stated, and a co-resident relative could connect Patrick to household A or B), Patrick's marriage record, the death certificates of his children (which may name his father), his obituary and burial record, and naturalization papers. Any of these could name the father or link Patrick to one household. Conclusions are never final: a later record could change this finding.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

## Conclusion
A possible answer, not yet an established one: Patrick's father may have been Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County. No mother is identified. The evidence is a single indirect item and does not yet support a probable conclusion.

## Evidence
The 1850 U.S. census lists Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household headed by Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, family 91), Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Citation: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.

The source is an original record. The information about the relationship, however, is indirect and inferred: the 1850 census does not state relationships, no informant is identified, and the researcher inferred a possible parent-child tie from household position and shared surname. The household head's name is also from an unidentified informant (likely Thomas himself). Thomas's age of about 32 (born about 1818) is consistent with fatherhood of a five-year-old, which makes the tie plausible but does not establish it.

## Analysis
A same-surname child in an 1850 household could be a son, but equally a nephew, grandchild, younger relative or unrelated resident. Nothing in the record separates these alternatives. No second record corroborates the tie, and no record names a mother. The identity links reflect this: the link of the household record to Patrick is confident, but the parent-child link is rated speculative.

One discrepancy is noted for transparency, not registered as a conflict: the existing tree fact F1 (Birth, about 1845, place given as Ireland, citing the 1850 census) differs from the project objective's statement of a Pennsylvania birth. The 1850 census would record a birthplace, and this should be re-read against the image. It bears on whether the household record and the later 1908 decedent are the same man and should be settled when the death certificate is found.

## Tier
Possible. One original source with indirect, inferred information, no corroboration, no conflicts in the registered evidence, and research not declared exhaustive. Because named reachable records (the 1860 census and the 1908 death certificate) could confirm or refute the answer itself, the tier is capped here. Nothing is encoded in the tree: a possible parentage stays off the tree until it reaches probable.

## What could resolve it
The 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate (parents are commonly named by the informant), the 1860 and 1880 censuses (the 1880 census states relationship to head), baptism records of the Flynn family, and Thomas Flynn's estate records. Each remains to be searched, and the question stays open pending them.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Conclusion

Patrick Flynn (born 1845 in Ireland, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania) was the son of Thomas Flynn. The mother, Mary Brennan, is named by the same two sources but is tracked as a separate question.

## Direct evidence with primary information

1. **Baptismal register.** The St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church (County Tipperary) register records the baptism on 12 March 1845 of Patricius Flynn, son of Thomas Flynn and Maria Brennan. The priest, Rev. Michael O'Connor, recorded it with the parents present. This is an original record, with primary information and direct evidence of parentage. Citation: St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church (County Tipperary, Ireland), baptismal register, entry for Patricius Flynn, son of Thomas Flynn and Maria Brennan, baptized 12 March 1845; National Library of Ireland Catholic Parish Registers, microfilm 04173/04, image 287; digital image, NationalLibrary.ie, accessed 4 May 2026.
2. **Family Bible.** The Flynn family Bible (Dublin imprint 1840) records the birth of Patrick Flynn, 1845, son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Brennan. The entries are in a single contemporaneous hand, written by the father, and the Bible's imprint predates them. It is an original record with primary information, and a different recorder and record type from the baptism, so it is independent of it. Its provenance links it to our Patrick: it descended from Patrick Flynn (d. 1908) to his daughter, the wife of James Brown, and down her line. Citation: Flynn family Bible (Holy Bible, Dublin imprint 1840), birth and family record pages, entry for Patrick Flynn, b. 1845, son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Brennan; original descended from Patrick Flynn (d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania) through his daughter, the wife of James Brown, to its present holder, a descendant in her line; digital images examined 4 May 2026.

## Corroboration

- **1908 death certificate** (Pennsylvania Department of Health, certificate no. 4521, Patrick Flynn; accessed 3 May 2026) names Thomas Flynn as father. The informant was his son-in-law James Brown, so the information is secondary, but it is direct and agrees.
- **1850 and 1860 censuses** (Schuylkill County; 1850 dwelling 84, family 91, NARA M432 roll 810; 1860 dwelling 112, family 119, NARA M653 roll 1141) show Patrick, age 5 and then 15, in the household of Thomas Flynn. These censuses did not state relationships, so this is indirect evidence of indeterminate quality. It is consistent with the conclusion and ties the Irish-born child to the Pennsylvania household.
- The Ancestry 1850 index is a derivative copy of the same census and adds no independent weight.
- A probate search for Thomas Flynn (Schuylkill County, 1870-1890) found nothing. This neither supports nor contradicts the conclusion.

## Conflict

The death certificate gives Pennsylvania as the birthplace, while both censuses, the baptism and the Bible point to Ireland (conflict c_001, resolved). The informant was a son-in-law reporting decades later, so the Ireland evidence outweighs him. This dispute does not bear on parentage: the death certificate names the same father.

## Identity

The baptized Patricius, the Bible's Patrick, the censuses' Patrick and the decedent of 1908 agree on name, birth year (1845), Irish birth and father's name. The Bible's descent through the decedent's own daughter connects it to him.

## Tier

Two independent original sources with primary information agree on the relationship, corroborated by further sources, with no contradicting evidence and the only conflict resolved. Search was reasonably exhaustive. The finding is proved, subject to revision if new evidence arises.

The baptized Patricius, the Bible's Patrick, the censuses' Patrick and the decedent of 1908 agree on name, birth year (1845), Irish birth and father's name. The Bible's descent through the decedent's own daughter connects it to him.

Two independent original sources with primary information agree on the relationship, corroborated by further sources, with no contradicting evidence and the only conflict resolved. Search was reasonably exhaustive. The finding is proved, subject to revision if new evidence arises.
